title: Open source semi: Windrose puts its electric truck online, for free
content:
Electric Semi Truck
Windrose
open source
Jo Borrás
| Sep 17 2026 - 5:03 am PT
This week, Windrose founder and CEO Wen Han made heavy truck history by putting the CAD models for all 1,023 parts from the X9D01 base model of his Windrose E700 Class 8 electric truck online. For free.
Windrose 3D Viewer
gives enthusiasts, engineers, and curious lookie-loos a detailed, fully inclusive look at the design and engineering behind
the company’s incredibly capable battery electric semi truck
– but it also gives someone else, someone much more important, a peek behind the curtain:
Windrose’ customers
And in doing so, Windrose is raising the bar for what customers should expect when it comes to serviceability.
A Class 8 truck works for fifteen years. A fleet buying from a manufacturer founded four years ago carries a risk it rarely states out loud. “What happens to parts supply in year twelve?” Every new entrant has been asked this question and none of us has had a good answer, because the honest answer has always been, “trust us.”
This is a better answer.
WINDROSE CEO
With the geometry of more than 1,000 proprietary components published online
, Windrose’s CEO argues that any competent fab shop should be able to machine a mount, fold a bracket, or fabricate a panel that may be needed for repair.
After spending the better part of two afternoons going over the Windrose 3D Viewer models with an ex-Ford engineer and a pair of high-end tuners telling me the same thing, I’m a believer.
It’s all there
E700 CAD drawing, via Windrose.
The open source move is more than an impressive bit of corporate transparency
; it’s a potential game-changer for ownership. If you know how to make the parts you need, you can ensure that the Windrose truck you buy today won’t become an expensive paperweight if the company goes the way of
Bollinger
LION Electric
And if the battery packs can be repaired or even remanufactured independently
, the potential service life gets even longer, still.
And Wen, to his credit, gets it. “Our customers are not dependent on us being reachable or being responsive, or being here,” he wrote,
in a post on LinkedIn
. “Our trucks should outlive our ability to support them. This is how we make that true.”
You can read Windrose’ terms and conditions for use of its parts data, below, then let us know what you think of Windrose’ latest bid to gain some market trust in the comments.
Service, repair, replacement parts and modification of a Windrose vehicle: free. No fee, no permission, no notification. That holds for owners, for independent workshops, and for anyone making parts for them. Independent repairers already have these rights in the EU and most US states; we are removing the practical obstacle rather than granting a favour.
Manufacturing vehicles from these designs: by agreement with us. Talk to us and we will be reasonable, but it is a conversation, not a download
Format: native PRT, unconverted, 3.54 GB. A STEP or JT export records final geometry only. The native file carries the feature tree — sketch constraints, driving and driven dimensions, parametric relations, and the order in which the part was built. That is design intent, and it does not survive export. A shop reproducing a part twelve years from now will want the former, not the latter.
Also included: an assembly tree of 1,920 parent-child relationships across 97 assemblies, and a manifest giving part names, systems and per-vehicle quantities.

title: Solid-state battery maker Factorial secures another big partnership
content:
Solid-state batteries
solid-state battery
Factorial Energy
Peter Johnson
| Sep 17 2026 - 4:00 am PT
Solid-state battery specialist
Factorial Energy
is teaming up with Mitsui Kinzoku, one of the few companies producing sulfide-based solid electrolytes, to scale up the promising new technology.
Factorial Energy finds a new solid-state battery partner
US-based Factorial Energy has been at the forefront of solid and semi-solid-state battery development.
Through its proprietary FEST (Factorial Electrolyte System Technology) and Solstice platforms, the company aims to solve one of the biggest hurdles in commercializing solid-state batteries: Scalable manufacturing.
After announcing its new partnership with Mitsui Kinzoku, Factorial CEO Siyu Huang said, “Batteries are a key technology for realizing an electrified society,” but added, “Significant technical challenges still remain.”
Mitsui Kinzoku is a leading producer and one of the few with sulfide-based solid electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries.
The Japanese manufacturing giant is the global leader in ultra-thin copper foil, accounting for about 90% of the semiconductor market for that type of foil.
It also developed
, an argyrodite sulfide solid electrolyte designed for all-solid-state batteries. Mitsui Kinzoku will mass-produce the solid electrolyte at a dedicated plant in Saitama, Japan.
Factorial all-solid-state EV battery (Source: Factorial)
The new alliance brings together Factorial’s Solstice all-solid-state platform with Mitsui Kinzoku’s electrolyte technology.
Factorial said the partnership “positions Solstice at the center of an industry-wide push toward commercializing all-solid-state batteries.” It’s expected to be key as Factorial accelerates global scale-up of its Solstice platform.
Factorial solid-state batteries (Source: Stellantis)
Battery innovation takes teamwork
“Battery innovation can’t be done by one single company,” Huang said, adding, “We’re not just building a battery. We’re building the connective thread that helps the whole industry move forward together.”
Factorial’s new alliance with Mitsui Kinzoku is the latest in a series of recent developments as it works to mass-produce the new battery tech.
The solid-state battery maker received investments from POSCO Future M and IQT. In January, it received its first commercial order for passenger vehicles, followed by its first aerospace order in July.
Dodge Charger EV with Factorial’s FEST solid-state batteries begins on-road testing in North America (Source: Stellantis)
Factorial has partnerships with major automakers including Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and Hyundai for electric vehicles. It also plans to supply solid-state batteries for aerospace, defense, and robotics.
According to Factorial, the Solstice platform has up to 450 Wh/kg, or 80% higher energy density than traditional lithium-ion batteries. It also remains stable at temperatures up to 194°F (90°C).
Earlier this year, the company launched the
first commercial solid-state battery program in the US
through a collaboration with Karma Automotive.
A modified Mercedes EQS with solid-state batteries travels 750 miles (1,205 km) on a single charge (Source: Mercedes-Benz)
Its solid-state battery cells have already demonstrated high energy density, fast charging, and impressive driving range in real-world conditions.
A year ago, Mercedes-Benz drove a modified EQS
for over 745 miles
(1,200 km) using Factorial’s 106 solid-state cells.
Factorial also announced it had
begun testing
its FEST solid-state battery cells in North America through a collaboration with Stellantis. The cells were used to power a Dodge Charger Daytona prototype.
Stellantis said last year that Factorial’s 77Ah FEST cells achieved an energy density of 375 Wh/kg over more than 600 cycles.
Stellantis and Factorial’s solid-state battery module (Source: Stellantis)
The cells also achieved a discharge rate of up to 4C while delivering ultra-fast charging from 15% to 90% in 18 minutes, while maintaining performance in extreme temperatures ranging from -22°F to 113°F (-30°C to 45°C).
Factorial and SK On
signed an MOU
in July to bring Factorial’s solid-state battery cell technology to SK On’s extensive global manufacturing network. SK On supplies batteries for Hyundai Motor Group, Ford, and Volkswagen.
During an interview with
The New York Times
last December, Huang said that Factorial’s solid-state EV batteries could be used in EVs as early as 2027.
They will likely be used first in high-performance or luxury electric vehicles, before rolling out to mass-market models.

title: Taiwan adds carbon-footprint requirement to high-efficiency PV module standard - pv magazine Global
content: Taiwan’s Bureau of Standards, Metrology and Inspection (BSMI) has updated its voluntary high-efficiency PV module specification to include a product carbon-footprint threshold, alongside tighter mechanical-load and aging-test requirements. BSMI published an updated version of its PV technical specifications earlier this month as part of the country’s voluntary product certification (VPC) system for solar modules. The update incorporates carbon-footprint reporting and verification requirements into the specification, while the applicable carbon-footprint thresholds are set through a separate BSMI factory-inspection rule published in May 2026. The September specification also tightens mechanical durability testing and adds a new accelerated-aging protocol. The new specification references carbon-footprint compliance, while the numerical thresholds are established through the May factory-inspection rule. Applicants seeking certification must conduct a product carbon-footprint inventory using life-cycle-assessment methodology under CNS 14040 and CNS 14044, Taiwan’s national standards, and quantify the result following ISO 14067:2018 and its Taiwanese counterpart, CNS 14067:2021. Crystalline-silicon modules must not exceed 0.12 kg CO2e/W, while thin-film modules face a threshold of 0.85 kg CO2e/W. BSMI said it may revoke a factory-inspection report if verified production data fail to meet the applicable threshold. The carbon-footprint requirement reflects a broader policy trend toward incorporating carbon metrics into PV qualification schemes. France’s Évaluation Carbone Simplifiée provides a useful comparison: administered through certification body Certisolis, it links verified module carbon data to public tenders and renewable-energy support mechanisms, with some categories citing thresholds around 550 kg CO2e/kWp. The two systems use different units – Taiwan measures per watt, France per kilowatt-peak – as well as different methodologies, so the figures are not directly comparable without accounting for those differences. The European Union does not currently apply its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to solar modules. CBAM’s definitive regime, which took effect this year, covers iron and steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen. The European Commission has proposed extending the mechanism to some downstream goods containing carbon-intensive steel or aluminum, a proposal still under review by the European Parliament as of September, but there is no general EU-wide carbon-footprint certification requirement for PV modules equivalent to Taiwan’s updated rule. For Taiwan, the new specification also raises the nation’s mechanical-load testing requirement to 5,400 pascals, a static load test applied to a module’s front and rear surfaces under CNS 61215-2, Taiwan’s adoption of the international IEC 61215-2 design-qualification standard. In IEC-based module testing, such load levels are typically associated with heavy snow-load conditions, compared with a baseline of 2,400 pascals used for standard wind-load qualification. The test does not by itself determine whether a module is suitable for a specific project site, which depends on mounting design, local structural codes and additional site-specific engineering factors. A new accelerated-aging test requires modules to withstand cumulative simulated irradiance of 756 kilowatt-hours per square meter, delivered through repeated thermal and light-exposure cycles, with output degradation limited to under 5% by the end of the test. BSMI’s specification describes this cumulative exposure level as equivalent to approximately five years of outdoor irradiance exposure. The test screens specifically for irradiance-driven degradation, such as light-induced degradation and discoloration, and does not by itself establish a full 25-year service-life curve. Other failure mechanisms, including thermal cycling, humidity-freeze stress and mechanical fatigue, are evaluated through separate, longstanding test protocols. PV Taiwan Plus certification remains part of Taiwan’s voluntary product-certification system rather than a blanket legal requirement for all modules sold in the country. Whether a specific government procurement program, subsidy scheme or project-approval process requires certification depends on that program’s own rules. The updated specification arrives as Taiwan pushes to expand solar deployment while tightening resilience and land-use rules. The government is targeting 20 GW of installed solar capacity by November 2026, and mechanical durability has taken on added urgency after Typhoon Danas damaged more than 135,000 panels in 2025, prompting manufacturers such as TSEC to launch typhoon-resistant, locally produced glass-glass modules rated for high wind loads. title: First Solar drops TOPCon patent complaint - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The thin-film manufacturer withdrew its Section 337 filing before the USITC following new Section 232 import restrictions, while federal court patent battles against domestic and foreign manufacturers move forward.
Ryan Kennedy
17 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Manufacturing
U.S. solar manufacturer First Solar has announced a recalibration of its intellectual property enforcement strategy, opting to voluntarily withdraw its Section 337 complaint before the U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC).
Under Section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, the USITC investigates claims of unfair competition and patent infringement involving imported goods. If the commission finds a violation, it holds the power to issue exclusion orders that block infringing products from entering the United States entirely. In its initial complaint, First Solar sought to stop imports of Tunnel Oxide Passivated Contact (TOPCon) solar cells and modules made by competitors. Had the USITC ruled in First Solar’s favor, an exclusion order would have abruptly halted shipments from major international suppliers, severely choking domestic equipment supply and slowing project deployments across the solar industry at a time when developers are rushing to meet historic electricity demand.
First Solar cited recent federal
Section 232
actions placed on imported polysilicon and its derivatives as the catalyst for withdrawing the trade action, arguing that the new trade measures establish protection at the border and allow the company to focus directly on domestic legal remedies.
Notably, First Solar does not manufacture TOPCon solar panels itself. The Arizona-headquartered company specializes exclusively in thin-film Cadmium Telluride (CdTe) semiconductor technology, a completely distinct photovoltaic platform that does not use silicon wafers. Instead, First Solar acquired its extensive TOPCon patent portfolio through its 2013 purchase of TetraSun, leaving it holding key intellectual property over an N-type silicon technology widely used by its primary commercial rivals.
While the trade investigation is being dropped, First Solar confirmed it will continue pursuing active patent infringement lawsuits in U.S. District Court against several major solar manufacturers, including affiliates of Canadian Solar, JinkoSolar, Trina Solar, and T1 Energy. Those federal court cases had been stayed pending the outcome of the USITC process.
“The Trump Administration’s Section 232 action helps level the playing field at the border, and we are more determined than ever to enforce our IP rights and defend the rule of law here at home,” said Jason Dymbort, General Counsel at First Solar. “This is a procedural decision that clears the way for our pending suits to move forward and for additional suits we anticipate filing.”
Respondents named in the initial trade complaint pushed back against the merits of the withdrawn filing. In a statement addressing the withdrawal, domestic manufacturer T1 Energy welcomed the end of the USITC investigation.
“First Solar can attempt to spin the narrative, but the facts are straightforward,” said Russell Gold, spokesman for T1 Energy. “T1 Energy is the only American company that both owns patents to high efficiency TOPCon solar and currently manufactures TOPCon solar modules. We are pleased that First Solar voluntarily withdrew what we believe was a flawed Sec. 337 complaint that would have slowed needed energy production at a time when the United States needs all the affordable electricity we can produce.”
First Solar’s TOPCon patent portfolio includes issued patents covering cell architectures across the U.S., Canada, China, Europe, and Asia extending through 2030 and beyond. The withdrawal of the USITC trade complaint allows stayed district court litigation to resume, setting up the next phase of the industry-wide patent dispute over high-efficiency TOPCon manufacturing.

title: Bangladesh launches $123 million rooftop solar fund - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Bangladesh has launched a $123 million fund to provide concessional financing for rooftop solar and other renewable energy projects. The government is also seeking international funding to install 4 GW of rooftop solar before next summer.
Syful Islam
17 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Residential
Bangladesh’s Renewable Energy Development Policy 2026–2030 targets a 20% share of renewables in Bangladesh’s electricity generation mix by 2030.
Bangladesh has established a $123 million fund to finance rooftop solar and other renewable energy projects as the government seeks to address persistent power shortages.
The Finance Division announced the fund on Wednesday. The money has been reallocated from the development budget for the current fiscal year.
The Power Division is also seeking financing from development partners, including the Asian Development Bank, the Japan International Cooperation Agency and the World Bank. The government aims to deploy 4 GW of rooftop solar capacity before next summer.
The new fund will provide concessional loans for renewable energy projects at the residential, institutional and industrial levels.
Finance Division Joint Secretary Anarul Kabir said the initiative is intended to provide affordable financing on favorable terms for renewable energy installations, including rooftop PV systems.
The Renewable Energy Development Policy 2026–2030 targets a 20% share of renewables in Bangladesh’s electricity generation mix by 2030, with rooftop solar expected to support the expansion.
Infrastructure Development Company Ltd. (IDCOL), Bangladesh Infrastructure Finance Fund Ltd. (BIFFL) and Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF) will distribute the funds.
Eligible projects include new, expanded and upgraded renewable energy installations. These include net-metered rooftop PV systems, solar home systems, industrial solar arrays and solar irrigation pumps.
Bangladesh currently has 1,852 MW of installed renewable energy capacity, including 1,473 MW of solar.

title: South Korea's new agrivoltaics law sets 30-year permit ceiling - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
South Korea has enacted its first dedicated agrivoltaics law, extending the maximum project period to 30 years from a previously reported 23-year framework, but key technical requirements remain undecided pending additional regulations.
Brian Publicover
17 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Agrivoltaics
South Korea’s Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs (MAFRA) said this week that the country has issued a new agrivoltaics law, set to take effect Dec. 17, following the
bill’s passage through the National Assembly
The law creates the country’s first dedicated legal framework for combining solar generation with continued agricultural production. MAFRA is responsible for implementing the act.
The enacted statute sets a maximum project period of up to 30 years, which is an increase from the 23-year framework reported when the bill passed the National Assembly.
The precise duration granted to any individual project will be determined by local authorities under a future presidential decree, according to ministry statements. The 30-year ceiling replaces South Korea’s previous eight-year temporary land-use permit regime, which
researchers had identified as a barrier to project financing
The law restricts eligibility to operate an agrivoltaic project to three categories. The first is local farmers who have continuously resided in the relevant area and can demonstrate at least three years of agricultural management. The second is resident-participation cooperatives formed by at least 10 local residents. The third is qualifying agricultural corporations operating within designated renewable energy zones.
The law does not necessarily bar all forms of external capital or financing arrangements – it specifically restricts who may hold the licensed project-operator status. Eligible farmland is limited to land outside Agricultural Promotion Zones, or land within those zones that has been separately designated a Renewable Energy Zone, a designation established under South Korea’s framework on the restructuring of rural spaces.
The nonprofit group Solutions for Our Climate said in May that Agricultural Promotion Zones cover approximately 47% of South Korea’s total farmland, a figure drawn from external land-use data rather than the statute itself. The enacted law does not restate or revise that estimate; it only sets the legal pathway by which land in such zones could become eligible.
The law requires project operators to continue agricultural production every year under an approved farming plan, and imposes maintenance and record-keeping obligations on the underlying solar equipment. But the legislation leaves the technical details to a presidential decree that hasn’t been issued yet – things like exact limits on shading, how tall structures can be, spacing between supports.
What the law itself says now appears to be narrower in scope. Ultimately, local authorities have to check that a project’s structure does not block farm machinery or cut off too much sunlight.
Policy and industry materials have floated a shading limit near 30%, minimum structure heights around 2.5 meters and support spacing near 4 meters as likely benchmarks, though none of these figures are confirmed requirements of the enacted law.
South Korea now joins a small group of countries with dedicated agrivoltaics legislation. France’s
2023 APER law
set a national legal definition for agrivoltaics, including a requirement that yields on covered land stay at roughly 90% of a reference plot, but questions remain in France over how
agrivoltaic project revenues are shared with local communities
Italy’s framework also
requires sites to maintain at least 80% of standard agricultural output
, but its thresholds differ from South Korea’s. Japan, meanwhile, has run a national agrivoltaics guidance framework since 2021, but its rules stop short of a dedicated statute.
The new South Korean law arrives as the country moves to expand financial support for dual-use solar. MAFRA has proposed nearly doubling
government funding for factory rooftop solar and agrivoltaics
to KRW 1.8 trillion ($1.3 billion) in a newly issued 2027 budget, and the country’s largest single-site solar project under development, the
Haenam solar complex
, includes 10 MW earmarked as agricultural PV capacity.

title: Spain launches capacity market as grid investment rises above €17 billion - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Spain is introducing a new mechanism to remunerate generation, battery storage and demand for providing firm capacity and flexibility, while increasing planned electricity grid investment through 2030 to more than €17 billion ($19.5 billion).
Pilar Sánchez Molina
17 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
Spain will introduce a capacity market for the peninsular electricity system, creating a new revenue mechanism for battery storage, generation and demand-side resources while the government increases planned electricity grid investment through 2030 to more than €17 billion.
The Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge (MITECO) announced the capacity market regulation on Sept. 16, with the ministerial order due to be published in the Official State Gazette (BOE). The mechanism is designed to ensure security of supply and support the integration of additional renewable generation.
The capacity market will remunerate generation, storage and demand resources for providing firm capacity and flexibility. Participants will receive payments for remaining available to inject electricity into the grid or reduce consumption when required by the system operator, Red Eléctrica.
Capacity will be awarded through technology-neutral auctions based on firm capacity in MW and price in €/MW per year, using a pay-as-bid system. Generation projects must meet an emissions limit of 550 g of CO₂/kWh, as well as the firmness and flexibility requirements specified for each auction, and cannot receive regulated remuneration.
For new investments, only renewable energy, storage and demand projects will be eligible. The government said this is intended to direct new capacity toward non-fossil technologies.
The market will have three auction mechanisms. The main auction will be open to existing installations and new projects, with service periods of one year for existing installations, up to 15 years for new investments, and between one and 10 years for new demand.
The main auctions will depend on five-year system coverage assessments identifying future firm-capacity requirements. The longer contracts available to new projects are intended to provide revenue visibility for investment and financing.
An annual adjustment auction will be restricted to operational installations and provide capacity for 12-month periods to address short-term system requirements. A transitional auction will provide firm capacity until services awarded through the main auctions begin, with annual service periods.
Consumers and electricity suppliers will fund the capacity market through differentiated unit charges based on tariff segments and time periods. Consumption during periods of greatest system stress, which will account for no more than 10% of the year, will bear a larger share of the cost. The design is intended to encourage consumers to shift electricity use away from peak periods.
The mechanism will also include a secondary market for capacity rights and obligations awarded through the auctions, allowing them to be transferred between eligible installations. Red Eléctrica and the National Commission of Markets and Competition (CNMC) will oversee verification and compliance.
Grid investment
Alongside the capacity market, Spain is increasing planned investment in its electricity transmission network through 2030.
The proposed 2030 transmission network plan initially included €13.6 billion of investment. Following the review of 2,566 submissions received during the public consultation, the planned investment has increased by more than 30% to more than €17 billion, or 144% above the investment level in the current plan.
Demand accounted for 41% of the proposals received during the consultation, compared with 40% for generation and 19% for storage.
The revised plan increases the number of transmission network positions intended to serve new demand on distribution networks by 52% to 300. Positions for direct consumption connected to the transmission network will increase by 12% to 162, while positions planned for rail corridors and port electrification will rise by 75% to 59.
The plan also includes 193 substations, 17% more than in the initial proposal, and 6,706 km of new transmission lines, an 11% increase. The length of existing networks scheduled for reinforcement will rise by 6% to 8,164 km.
The Spanish government said the expanded network plan is intended to accommodate growing electricity demand from industry, buildings and transport while supporting additional renewable generation and storage.
The capacity market and network plan therefore address two separate requirements for Spain’s power system: the grid investment provides additional network infrastructure, while the capacity mechanism creates a new payment stream for resources able to provide electricity or reduce demand when the system requires it.

title: Scientists build 17%-efficient semi-transparent perovskite solar cell based on sputter-resistant aluminum oxide layer - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers replaced the conventional 20 nm SnOₓ buffer layer with just 3 nm of ALD-deposited AlOₓ, which protected inverted perovskite cells from ITO sputtering damage while maintaining efficient charge extraction.
The resulting devices achieved efficiencies above 17% in semi-transparent cells and 26% in perovskite-silicon tandems, while reducing material use and fabrication time.
Lior Kahana
17 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Schematic of the solar cell
An international research team has proposed using a thin aluminum oxide (AlOₓ) buffer layer in inverted perovskite solar cells to suppress interfacial charge recombination and protect the perovskite, thereby improving both efficiency and operational stability.
Deposited via atomic layer deposition (ALD), the layer sits between the buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) electron transport layer (ETL) and the sputtered indium tin oxide (ITO) contact.
“The novelty of this research lies in demonstrating that the conventional 10 nm to 20 nm thick SnO₂ buffer layer, typically used to prevent sputter damage, can be replaced by a much thinner, yet more uniform AlOₓ layer,” corresponding author Stephanie Essig told
pv magazine
. “It was surprising to find that a 3 nm thick AlOₓ layer allows efficient charge-carrier extraction across the C₆₀/ITO interface.”
“We plan to further optimize the transparent conductive oxide (TCO) sputtering process to mitigate sputter damage, alongside extended stability testing of device performance,” she said.
To evaluate the buffer layers, the researchers fabricated semi-transparent inverted perovskite solar cells with ALD-deposited AlOₓ or SnOₓ layers between the C₆₀ electron transport layer and a sputtered ITO electrode. They tested AlOₓ thicknesses of 1.5 nm, 3 nm, 5 nm, 8 nm, and 15 nm, comparing their performance with buffer-free cells and reference devices featuring SnOₓ layers of 3 nm, 10 nm, and 20 nm.
The team also investigated the effects of ALD deposition temperature by comparing AlOₓ layers deposited at 75 C and 80 C. It optimized the process using a repeated water-pulse sequence.
The scientists built the top inverted cell with a glass and indium tin oxide (ITO) substrate coated with a Me-4PACz hole-selective layer and silicon oxide nanoparticles. A roughly 1.4-nm aluminum oxide (AlOₓ) interlayer was placed between the perovskite absorber and a 20-nm C₆₀ electron-transport layer. The device was completed with a 25-nm atomic-layer-deposited tin oxide layer and a 130-nm silver electrode. A 100-nm lithium fluoride coating on the glass side served as an antireflective layer.
The scientists used microscopy, spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, photoluminescence, and electrical measurements to assess the layers’ morphology, coverage, chemical composition, resistance to sputter damage, and charge-transport properties. They then incorporated the optimized 3 nm AlOₓ layer into monolithic two-terminal perovskite-silicon tandem cells and compared their performance with that of cells featuring a conventional 20 nm SnOₓ buffer layer.
The results showed that, under low-power magnetron sputtering conditions, a 3 nm AlOₓ buffer layer effectively suppressed sputtering-induced damage, while a 1.5 nm layer did not. Devices featuring the 3 nm AlOₓ layer performed similarly to those with a 20 nm SnOₓ layer, achieving power conversion efficiencies of more than 17% in semi-transparent perovskite cells and more than 26% in perovskite-silicon tandem devices.
The researchers said the suitability of thin AlOₓ as a sputter-resistant buffer layer offers several advantages, including a dense and uniform ALD process, lower material consumption, and faster fabrication of future perovskite tandem and semi-transparent devices.
The research, “Sputter-resistant aluminum oxide layer enables robust perovskite tandem solar cells,” was published in
Materials Today
. Scientists from Germany’s
University of Stuttgart
Forschungszentrum Jülich
Solarlab Aiko Europe
, as well as Portugal’s
INL – International Iberian Nanotechnology Laboratory
, contributed to the study.
Essig highlighted first author Seyma Topcu’s role in advancing the research and said the team plans to conduct follow-up studies.

title: China targets perovskite solar, advanced batteries in five-year plan - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
China has identified perovskite solar and next-generation batteries as strategic priorities in its 2026-30 industrial roadmap. The plan also calls for tighter oversight of manufacturing capacity and price competition.
Vincent Shaw
17 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT)
China has outlined a new five-year industrial roadmap for solar, batteries and energy electronics, combining support for next-generation technologies with tighter controls on manufacturing capacity and price competition.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) released the Electronic Information Manufacturing Industry Development 15th Five-Year Plan on Sept. 15. The document covers the 2026-30 period and identifies energy electronics as a potential source of growth for China’s electronics manufacturing industry.
The plan calls for closer coordination among solar, energy storage, end-use equipment and information technologies. It also sets out detailed technology roadmaps for PV and batteries, although it includes no specific manufacturing capacity or deployment targets for either sector.
For solar, Beijing wants manufacturers to continue improving high-efficiency crystalline silicon technology while accelerating the development and commercialization of perovskite tandem cells. The plan also calls for lower-energy production of high-purity polysilicon, larger and thinner wafers, more reliable module encapsulation and increasingly intelligent PV modules. It targets inverters, controllers and tracking systems for further digitalization and intelligent upgrades.
The document identifies perovskite materials, polyolefin elastomers and high-purity quartz sand as materials requiring further development and wider application.
It also targets markets beyond conventional utility-scale and distributed PV. The government wants to expand applications such as space-based and offshore solar, while encouraging emerging business models that combine PV generation with hydrogen, ammonia and methanol production.
For batteries, the plan says China should consolidate its competitive position in lithium-ion technology while advancing the industrialization of solid-state, sodium-ion and flow batteries, as well as fuel cells.
Policymakers called for the development and commercialization of high-energy-density solid-state batteries and low-cost, long-life sodium-ion batteries. They also identified solid electrolytes, silicon-carbon anodes, high-capacity cathode materials and composite current collectors as development priorities.
The roadmap extends beyond battery cells. It calls for improvements in power electronics and high-power converters, more efficient battery energy storage system integration and more precise control systems. The government also wants to advance storage management based on device-edge-cloud architectures and improve thermal management technologies, including phase-change materials, heat pipes and heat pumps.
The more significant policy shift, however, is on the supply side.
The plan calls for coordinated manufacturing capacity planning across industries, capacity early-warning mechanisms and comprehensive measures to address what Chinese policymakers describe as “involution-style” competition. It also seeks stronger safety management in the lithium-ion battery industry and better management of retired lithium batteries and PV modules.
The policy direction is not entirely new. Energy electronics guidelines published by six government bodies in 2023 already supported perovskite and tandem solar cells, along with solid-state, sodium-ion and flow batteries. The guidelines also warned manufacturers against excess capacity and “disorderly competition.”

title: PV inverters provide reactive power to Milan’s grid at night - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in Milan used PV inverters to supply 500 kVAr of reactive power to the distribution grid for four hours overnight. The trial showed that existing solar equipment can support voltage regulation even when it is not generating electricity.
Massimiliano Tripodo
17 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Inverters
Researchers at the
Polytechnic University of Milan
have used photovoltaic inverters to supply 500 kilovolt-ampere reactive (kVAr) of inductive reactive power to Milan’s distribution network.
The trial was intended to demonstrate how existing solar assets could support voltage regulation even when they are not generating electricity.
The demonstration took place on the night of Sept. 8-9 as part of Unareti’s MindFlex pilot project. The inverters connected to the PV systems at the university’s PoliGrid site supplied 500 kVAr of inductive reactive power for four consecutive hours, from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m.
The researchers verified delivery by comparing the reactive power exchanged at the grid connection point with a baseline representing PoliGrid’s expected behavior without activation. They calculated the baseline using average operating data recorded over the preceding days.
“The particularly interesting aspect is the use of photovoltaic inverters during the night,” Filippo Bovera, a researcher at the Politecnico di Milano and PoliGrid representative, told
pv magazine
. “At night, PV inverters are not required to convert the active power generated by solar modules. Their unused capacity can therefore be deployed to provide reactive power services to the grid.”
In the Milan trial, this enabled PoliGrid to use existing equipment at a low delivery cost, largely limited to inverter losses and wear, while generating additional revenue for the university.
Unareti, the distribution system operator owned by local utility A2A, procured the service through the MindFlex pilot market. The mechanism remunerates capacity availability in euros per kVAr per hour during a contracted period. For the trial, the availability window corresponded to Italy’s F3 tariff band, which runs from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. on weekdays.
The researchers said the demonstration shows how distributed energy resources, often regarded as an additional challenge for grid operators, could also support network management. When properly controlled and coordinated, inverters already connected to distribution networks can provide voltage and reactive power regulation, potentially improving power quality and reducing grid losses and overall system costs.
The ability of PV inverters to regulate reactive power is already technically established, according to the researchers. The principal obstacles to large-scale deployment are enabling the functionality across a wide asset base and ensuring that the resources can be controlled, aggregated and monetized.
Flexibility providers would need reliable communications infrastructure and monitoring and control platforms capable of coordinating large numbers of distributed devices. Distribution system operators would also require clear technical rules and market mechanisms to procure the services where they offer genuine network value. Automated dispatch systems would be needed to activate the resources in response to local grid conditions.
The researchers said that appropriate economic signals to support investment by flexibility providers and grid operators are still lacking. Reactive power is an inherently localized service, as its value depends on where the resource is connected to the network. A large aggregated inverter capacity would therefore not be sufficient on its own. Operators must also be able to activate that capacity at the times and locations where the distribution system operator needs it.
PoliGrid coordinated the PV inverters through LePo, an energy management system (EMS) developed by Maurizio Delfanti’s research group at the Politecnico di Milano’s Department of Energy in collaboration with the Energy and Environment Laboratory of Piacenza (LEAP).
The EMS uses forecasting and optimization tools for multi-energy systems to calculate the commands required to deliver the requested change in reactive power at the grid connection point. The Optimo internet-of-things architecture hosts and runs LePo, manages the resulting setpoints and transmits them to the PV control units and individual inverters.
For the trial, the inverter management systems were configured to remain operational at night, allowing the inverters to regulate reactive power when the PV arrays were not producing active power.
During activation, the system monitored reactive power at the point of delivery and continuously adjusted the inverter setpoints to deliver 500 kVAr relative to the baseline. The process involved more than setting the inverters to a fixed output of 500 kVAr, as the control system also had to account for the reactive power that the campus would have exchanged with the grid without the service.
The EMS also monitored the site’s other energy resources to assess the service’s effects on the wider energy system. According to the researchers, these effects are limited for reactive power regulation but become more significant when active power services are provided.
The participating PV systems use Huawei SUN2000 inverters controlled through Huawei SmartLogger 3000 units. Optimo’s IoT infrastructure, supported by ComAp devices, enables communication between the SmartLogger units and the EMS.
The test formed part of SIMBIOsi, a project funded by the Italian Ministry of Environment and Energy Security (MASE).

title: Global residential storage market to hit 46.1 GWh in 2026 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
InfoLink Consulting expects global residential energy storage capacity additions to reach 46.1 GWh in 2026, led by Europe, Oceania, and Asia. Fox ESS, Sigenergy, and Deye ranked as the top three suppliers by shipment volume in the first half of 2026.
InfoLink
17 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
Europe remains a key contributor to the global residential energy storage market, with capacity additions projected to reach 15.4 GWh.
According to InfoLink Consulting’s latest Global Residential Energy Storage Market and Shipment Database, global residential energy storage capacity additions are projected to reach 46.1 GWh in 2026.
Europe remains a key contributor to the global residential energy storage market, with capacity additions projected to reach 15.4 GWh. Established markets such as Germany, Italy, and Austria continue to perform strongly, while the Netherlands and the UK are seeing significant growth driven by policy support. Eastern European markets, led by Ukraine, are also rapidly emerging as growth markets.
In a shift from Europe’s previous dominance, capacity additions in Oceania and Asia are gradually approaching those in Europe.
Growth in Oceania has been driven primarily by Australia’s Cheaper Home Batteries Program, launched on July 1, 2025. Supported by substantial subsidies, Australia is expected to become the world’s largest single-country residential energy storage market in 2026.
Growth in Asia is led by Pakistan in South Asia, the Philippines and Vietnam in Southeast Asia, and Japan. In markets such as Pakistan and the Philippines, frequent power outages and high residential electricity prices are also driving rapid growth in residential energy storage demand.
The Americas, the Middle East and Africa remain relatively small markets. Demand in the Americas is centered on the U.S., while some Latin American countries are shifting from residential PV-only demand toward PV-plus-storage. In the Middle East and Africa, key markets include South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Iraq, and Israel, where demand is driven mainly by backup power during outages and fully off-grid power supply.
The database compiles and presents the global shipment ranking of residential energy storage suppliers in the first half of 2026 (H1 2026), along with detailed shipment rankings across the five regions mentioned above. Fox ESS, Sigenergy, and Deye ranked as the top three global suppliers by shipments, with market shares of 11.5%, 11.3%, and 11.0%, respectively.
Fox ESS and Sigenergy hold leading market shares in both Europe and Oceania. Deye benefits from its strong presence in European markets such as Ukraine and Poland, as well as Pakistan, South Africa, and other markets across Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
Even among leading suppliers, no player has established an overwhelming market share advantage, and the gaps between manufacturers remain narrow. The market remains highly fragmented, with the competitive landscape still unsettled.
The database also assesses product and application trends in the 2026 residential energy storage market, highlighting five key trends.
I. Adoption of residential PV-plus-storage all-in-one systems is rising.
Stackable solutions from suppliers such as Sigenergy and GoodWe have gained strong traction due to their highly integrated design, space efficiency, ease of installation, and flexible capacity configurations. More suppliers are also launching similar products, including Sungrow’s PowerHarbor and Huawei Digital Power’s LUTERRA S2, unveiled at Intersolar Europe 2026.
II. Residential energy storage suppliers are expanding into C&I and balcony micro-storage.
Despite strong growth in 2026, suppliers are seeking new growth drivers, with these fast-growing, early-stage segments becoming preferred expansion targets. Suppliers have also been launching new products in these segments, while Sigenergy, Ginlong, KSTAR, and others have continued to secure C&I storage orders and bring projects online this year.
III. Integrated whole-home energy solutions combining PV, storage, EV charging, and heat pumps are gaining traction.
As EVs and heat pumps become more widely adopted, household loads are becoming more diverse. Integrated solutions can coordinate energy use to minimize household electricity costs. On the hardware side, integrated PV-storage-charging systems are increasingly being deployed, with vehicle-to-home (V2H) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) applications being piloted. On the software side, energy management system (EMS) capabilities are becoming more intelligent, with AI gradually being incorporated into home energy management.
IV. AI capabilities and virtual power plant (VPP) connectivity are gaining attention in residential energy storage.
While these systems were previously used mainly to increase self-consumption and reduce high electricity bills, their value proposition is now expanding. As VPP applications deepen across Europe and Australia, end users are placing greater emphasis on VPP connectivity and AI-powered energy dispatch capabilities. Smarter battery dispatch and VPP response strategies can generate additional revenue for users, further shortening project payback periods.
V. Residential energy storage markets are showing increasingly differentiated product needs across regions.
As Asia, the Middle East and Africa, and Latin America continue to expand, their requirements differ markedly from those in mature markets such as Europe, North America, and Australia. These mature markets place greater emphasis on product appearance, conversion efficiency, smart features, service life and warranty terms, and brand strength. In Asia, Africa, and Latin America, cost-effectiveness is the priority. With limited local installation and after-sales resources in some regions, demand favors safe, low-voltage residential systems with manageable costs, as well as split systems that allow flexible cross-brand pairing of inverters and batteries.

title: China’s 500 MW solar plant stops power swings in 40 milliseconds
content: A company in China has reproduced and suppressed wideband oscillations at a 500-megawatt (MW) solar-plus-storage power plant in what is described as the world’s first field test of the technology.The test was conducted by Sungrow, a Hefei-based renewable energy company specializing in solar photovoltaics (PV) and energy storage systems. Intended to counter wideband oscillations, it took place at a plant in the Chinese province of Qinghai in September 2026. Wideband oscillations are rapid electrical fluctuations that can, in fact, destabilize renewable power systems. Additionally, they can force generating equipment to disconnect from the grid or shut down entirely. This unpredictable nature has so far made them difficult to reproduce at operating plants. Sungrow addressed this by deliberately triggering oscillations at a real-world plant. “For renewable energy to become a truly stable and reliable source of power, it is essential to develop autonomous fault self-healing and grid-support capabilities,” Pan Nian’an, chief engineer and chief expert at Sungrow, explained.Testing grid stabilityFor the test, the engineers established weak-grid conditions at the 500-MW plant, which uses Sungrow photovoltaic (PV) inverters. The team identified three factors involved in triggering the oscillations: the plant’s power output, the system short-circuit ratio (SCR), as well as inverter control parameters.They first adjusted these parameters, and then successfully reproduced a localized wideband oscillation in a controlled environment. They further tested how the PV inverters responded under different grid conditions. Sungrow completed a world-first oscillation suppression test at the plant.Credit: SungrowSungrow’s patented grid-strength adaptation technology identified the local grid strength within 40 milliseconds. The equipment then adjusted its control strategy to stabilize voltage and frequency.The demonstration also tested Sungrow’s grid-forming control technology. The system is designed to help power electronics actively support grid stability rather than simply follow existing grid conditions.According to the company, its grid-forming control strategy can maintain stable operation across an SCR range of 1 to 40, while also helping mitigate transient overvoltage.Outside the labWideband oscillations have previously been linked to major disruptions in power systems. For example, Germany’s BorWin1 offshore high-voltage direct current (HVDC) project experienced oscillations between 250 and 350 hertz in 2014. The incident damaged filter capacitors and contributed to a shutdown lasting around six months.A 2019 incident at the UK’s Hornsea offshore wind farm located in the North Sea, off the coast of England, also involved subsynchronous oscillations. The event led to widespread disconnections. Around 3.2 percent of system load was lost, affecting roughly one million users.Sungrow representatives believe that the latest test could help move oscillation-control technology beyond simulations and laboratories. It could eventually help renewable plants remain connected under extremely weak-grid conditions, cut lost generation, and increase the amount of electricity that facilities can export.Nian’an said that the company plans to continue developing wideband oscillation suppression, grid-forming controls, and technologies for coordinating multiple energy sources. “These efforts aim to support the stable grid integration and efficient utilization of renewable energy while strengthening the technical foundation for a secure and stable energy transition and next-generation power systems,” he concluded in a press release.

title: Giant submarine drone mothership being built in China, images suggest
content: China appears to be building a large surface vessel specifically designed to launch, recover, and support submarine-sized uncrewed underwater vehicles, according to satellite imagery analyzed by naval experts.The vessel is under construction at the Hudong-Zhonghua shipyard in Shanghai. Naval News, which first reported the development on September 15, assessed the ship as a likely purpose-built mothership for China’s emerging fleet of extra-extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicles, or XXLUUVs. The Telegraph subsequently reported similar findings from satellite imagery captured by U.S. defense intelligence company Vantor.A mothership for giant underwater dronesThe unusual vessel resembles a large amphibious ship but has features that appear tailored to handling exceptionally large underwater vehicles. Defence Security Asia reported that the ship is approximately 205 meters long and 27 meters wide, based on commercial satellite imagery dated September 15. Its stern reportedly contains a wet well-deck and a large cradle that can be lowered into the water using 12 vertical jack-up arms. An enclosed hangar forward of the well-deck could potentially accommodate up to four of China’s largest underwater drones.The arrangement would let the mothership keep the vehicles inside a protected hangar at sea or in port, then move them onto the cradle for launch and recovery. That would be considerably different from relying on specialized floating docks for every deployment.According to Naval News‘ H I Sutton, the internal hangar is one of the features that makes a dedicated drone-submarine support role the most plausible explanation for the vessel. The publication notes, however, that China has not publicly confirmed the ship’s purpose.China’s unusually large uncrewed submarinesThe suspected mothership is significant because China has already been testing underwater vehicles far larger than most known military UUVs. Two Chinese XXLUUV designs observed around Hainan are estimated at approximately 35 and 45 meters (115 and 148 feet) long. They are therefore substantially larger than the U.S. Navy’s Boeing Orca XLUUV, which is roughly 26 meters long overall.The Chinese vehicles have so far been associated with specialized floating docks used to transport and launch them for testing. A mobile mothership would potentially provide a more flexible way of moving the systems to different operating areas while carrying maintenance equipment and personnel with them.That could be particularly useful for vehicles intended to remain underwater for extended periods. Instead of returning to a fixed coastal facility after a mission, an XXLUUV could potentially be recovered by the ship, serviced and prepared for another deployment.What would the drones actually do?Their exact missions remain unknown. Analysts have suggested possible roles including intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, seabed monitoring, mine warfare and other long-range underwater missions. The large size could also provide space for substantial sensors, energy storage or modular payloads.Neither China nor the People’s Liberation Army Navy has publicly confirmed the operational specifications or intended weapons of the XXLUUVs. Claims about ranges, payloads, or specific combat missions therefore remain estimates rather than demonstrated capabilities.The suspected mothership itself may also have aviation facilities near the bow, according to imagery assessments, potentially providing another means of supporting operations. The Telegraph reported that the ship appears to have a hangar that could accommodate a helicopter.A new way to deploy underwater dronesThe most important development may therefore be the support infrastructure, rather than the ship alone. Large autonomous submarines are difficult to launch, recover, maintain and transport. A purpose-built mothership could combine those functions on a single mobile platform, potentially allowing China to move its largest uncrewed underwater systems farther from their existing test areas.At the same time, the vessel remains a work in progress. Satellite imagery cannot establish its final propulsion system, sensors, command architecture, payloads, or operational status. For now, the evidence simply suggests a specialized support ship being built around China’s unusually large underwater drones.

title: 2.5-GW Texas plant advances with Blue Energy's 300-MW reactor filing
content: Blue Energy has taken a major step toward building a new reactor in Texas by contacting federal regulators. The company has formally submitted the first part of its construction permit application to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). This filing focuses on installing a BWRX-300 small modular reactor at the Port of Victoria. It marks the start of an extensive federal review for a project that plans to blend nuclear energy with conventional natural gas.The proposed site near Victoria is designed as a hybrid 2.5-gigawatt power complex. Under this arrangement, Blue Energy intends to combine GE Vernova 7HA.02 gas turbines with advanced modular reactors. The facility is being developed to supply steady power for sectors that consume large amounts of electricity.To satisfy federal licensing standards, Blue Energy is following a phased submission strategy with regulators. The developers submitted the initial package first, but they must still compile technical field records before sending the rest.“The company expects to submit the remaining portion of the application in 2027 after they complete the NRC-mandated one calendar year of site-specific data collection,” added the company in a press release.Progressing with partnershipsWork on the Victoria facility has gathered speed over the past few months through close industrial ties. Blue Energy selected the BWRX-300 design earlier this year. In April 2026, the company signed a project acceleration agreement with GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy (GVH). The two partners moved even closer last month by signing an additional agreement to govern further development work on the 2.5-gigawatt complex. Under these arrangements, GVH provides crucial engineering work and technical information related to the reactor design.Company leaders say this steady cooperation is transforming a broad vision into physical reality. Jake Jurewicz, chief executive and co-founder of Blue Energy, pointed out that the partnership has progressed from technology selection to NRC permitting in only a few months. He said this milestone helps prove that their development approach can create a faster and repeatable path to deploy new nuclear power across the country.Broader fleet expansionThe filing also fits into an expanding regional pipeline for this reactor type. North of the border, Ontario Power Generation is already building a BWRX-300 unit at its Darlington site in Canada. In Tennessee, the Tennessee Valley Authority has submitted a construction permit application for the same design at Clinch River, where the NRC review is now approaching a decision.Jason Cooper, chief executive of GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, noted that these parallel efforts show what fleet deployment looks like in practice. Because multiple projects share identical engineering, licensing methods, and supply chains, teams can apply practical lessons directly from one build to the next. Cooper explained that this work is laying the groundwork for a broader fleet of BWRX-300 reactors both in the United States and internationally.

title: Plasma-electric method could turn CO2 into sustainable jet fuel
content: Scientists at Yale University have developed a system that combines plasma and electricity to transform carbon dioxide (CO2) into valuable chemicals, including methanol and butane. The study was carried out by Lea Winter, PhD, an assistant professor of chemical and environmental engineering at Yale. For the project Winter and her team tired coupling plasma with electrocatalysis. Plasma is often called the fourth state of matter, after solids, liquids, and gases. It is a highly energized gas in which electrons have been stripped from atoms, thus creating electrically charged particles.Winter said the approach could convert CO2 into fuels, pharmaceuticals, solvents, and other chemicals made from fossil fuels. “The sorts of multi-carbon products we generate with this approach are really useful for a lot of chemical industries,” she added. It could also produce precursor chemicals for sustainable aviation fuel. Breaking down CO2While CO2 is abundant, it has yet to be widely used to produce valuable products. That’s because it is a highly stable and inert molecule, which makes it difficult to convert into something useful without a lot of energy.Electrocatalysis is a promising solution. It utilizes electricity and a catalyst to drive chemical reactions that transform CO2 into other compounds. Still electrocatalysis on its own typically produces a relatively limited range of simple carbon products.That’s when the Yale team thought of pairing electrocatalysis with plasma, which contains highly energetic electrons. These electrons excite the CO2 molecules and weaken their bonds before they reach the electrocatalyst. The catalyst can then use the activated species to form different products.Winter said that plasma opens up chemical pathways that electrocatalysis cannot access on its own. However, these plasma-electrochemical processes typically rely on a water interface, which can limit their effectiveness.While the plasma activates the CO2 gas, the water can quench and neutralize the most reactive plasma species before they even reach the electrocatalyst. “It’s been challenging to figure out how to effectively couple plasma with catalysts in a way that allows us to actually see an effect of plasma – to get those plasma-excited species to participate in catalytic reactions,” Winter added.Overcoming the limitsTo overcome the issue, the scientists came up with a 3-phase interface that brings together gas, liquid and solid components. It simultaneously prevents the plasma from directly interacting with the water. The system relies on a gas diffusion electrode, which is a membrane made of the same type of material used in non-stick cookware. It is partly coated with a thin layer of copper that serves as the electrocatalyst. Its pores are large enough to allow the plasma particles to pass through to the electrocatalyst layer, meet the protons from the water, and drive the chemical reactions. According to the scientists, the method achieved some of the highest production rates yet for valuable alcohols and three- and four-carbon atoms. These products can be used for liquid fuels, pharmaceuticals and other valuable products.The team will next optimize the catalyst and experiment with alterative materials. The system also operates at room temperature and atmospheric pressure, which potentially makes it easier to commercialize. “And it’s a turnkey process,” Winter concluded in a press release. “You can switch it on or shut it off at will based on when electricity is available. It can also operate directly with intermittent renewable electricity, so we could see retrofitting an existing plant, and then you don’t need to build an entire new factory around it.”The study has been published in the journal Nature Catalysis.

title: Anduril unveils US Air Force's Fury fighter drone's new weapon lineup
content: Anduril Industries has shared new photos of its FQ-44A Fury uncrewed combat aircraft during weapons fit checks. The images, released on September 16, offer a clearer view of how the aircraft might carry guided bombs, rocket pods, and other external weapons as it moves toward production for the U.S. Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program.The photos show ongoing work to add external weapons to the Fury. Anduril is designing the aircraft to carry various weapons and mission gear, making it flexible for missions with crewed fighters.Fury shows off expanded weapons optionsAnduril captioned the new release “Fit for Fury” and said the sample setups “confirm Fury’s compatibility with a range of munitions.”The images show guided bombs and pods for 70mm rockets being attached to the aircraft. The planned weapons also include air-to-air and cruise missiles. Anduril has indicated that additional mission pods and other systems could be added, but some details have not been shared yet.The weapons work addresses an important part of the CCA effort as the Air Force develops uncrewed aircraft that can perform missions alongside existing fighters.Fit for Fury. Notional FQ-44 configurations confirm Fury’s compatibility with a range of munitions, including 500-pound class guided bombs, Small Diameter Bombs, air-launched cruise missiles, rocket pods, external targeting pods, and (many) more. Fight unfair. pic.twitter.com/wxtET00MtD— Anduril Industries (@anduriltech) September 15, 2026From prototype to production aircraftThe Fury, previously designated YFQ-44A during its prototype phase, is one of two aircraft selected by the Air Force in April 2024 for the first CCA increment. The Air Force also selected General Atomics’ YFQ-42A.The program aims to team uncrewed, semi-autonomous aircraft with crewed jets like the F-22 and F-35. These new aircraft will expand sensor range and add more weapons without needing another pilot.Anduril’s design traces its origins to Fury, a concept developed by Blue Force Technologies before Anduril acquired the company in 2023. The YFQ-44A completed ground testing at Beale Air Force Base in 2025 before making its first flight later that year from Southern California Logistics Airport in Victorville, California.In June 2026, the Air Force selected Anduril for the production phase, moving Fury toward its first batch of aircraft for more testing and future use. The value and size of the order have not been disclosed.Weapons testing already underwayThe latest fit checks follow earlier weapons tests with the Fury. Anduril and the Department of War have already run trials, including launching an RTX AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile.The Air Force plans to acquire at least 500 CCA aircraft in total to fly with crewed combat jets. In the first phase, however, the service has said it could order between 100 and 150 aircraft. It has not disclosed how many of those aircraft would be FQ-44s compared with YFQ-42As.The new images show how the Fury might help with strike missions once it is in service.CCA effort gains international interestThe CCA program is also getting international partners. The Netherlands officially joined in October 2025, opening the door for Dutch defense companies to take part in the project.Dutch participation could eventually support industrial cooperation and potential co-production of series-production aircraft.For the Air Force, the weapons integration work provides an early indication of how CCA aircraft could be used beyond their role as airborne sensors. The range of stores being evaluated suggests Fury is being prepared for missions requiring different types of weapons while operating as part of larger crewed and uncrewed formations.

title: Idaho site unveiled for first US campus-hosted 1,652°F microreactor
content: A new type of nuclear reactor will soon operate on an American university campus, replacing mechanical coolant pumps with sealed heat pipes. Idaho State University is preparing to commission the nation’s first university-hosted advanced microreactor, creating a live testing facility for next-generation nuclear technology.The machine is known as the Advanced Research and Test Reactor. It is being developed in partnership with NuCube Energy, an advanced nuclear technology company based in Idaho Falls. The project will sit at the university’s Business and Research Park, following ISU’s selection by the US Department of Energy under its Nuclear Reactor Innovation Center Launch Pad USA program.The core feature of NuCube’s reactor design is its heat-pipe cooling system. Most traditional nuclear reactors rely on mechanical pumps to circulate coolant through the core. By contrast, this microreactor uses heat pipes to passively carry thermal energy away from the fuel core and directly toward the power-conversion system. The reactor is built to run at extreme temperatures. Its architecture operates above 1,652°F (900°C), allowing it to supply both zero-carbon electricity and high-temperature heat. That level of heat is vital for heavy industrial processes that are difficult to decarbonize through ordinary power supplies.Technology validation for industry integrationTo prove the concept works safely under real-world operating conditions, NuCube recently partnered with Canadian Nuclear Laboratories on a dedicated research and development program. The two organizations are gathering experimental data and building computational models to predict how the heat pipes behave at temperatures over 900°C. NuCube says the findings will expand its validation database and help clear safety reviews for future commercial licensing.Because the system is factory-built and modular, it can be assembled before delivery. Hosting a working unit at ISU provides engineers and researchers with direct, physical access to evaluate the hardware during live runs. The university is already linking academic training with industry engineering. Sam Jeffries, an ISU graduate student with a decade of engineering experience, currently works as NuCube’s lab manager and test engineer, testing components while finishing his degree.Rare operational experienceThe university brings rare operational experience to the initiative. ISU has run its own research reactor on campus since 1965, making it one of only 24 universities in the United States with such a facility. It also offers the only undergraduate nuclear engineering degree in Idaho.On Wednesday, state officials and researchers met at the future construction site to mark the project’s formal launch. Idaho National Laboratory Deputy Director Todd Combs noted that while generations of students earned operator licenses on the 1965 reactor, hundreds more will train directly on this new microreactor to meet rising laboratory workforce needs.NuCube chief executive Cristian Rabiti described the venture as an effort to change how reactors are manufactured and deployed. Idaho Governor Brad Little told the gathering that Idaho is focused on building components, technology, and skilled workers for a wider nuclear renaissance. University President Robert Wagner concluded that the venture supports ISU’s long-term commitments under its Contract for Idaho as the institution marks its 125th anniversary.

title: Redback combat vehicle gets 40mm cannon and counter-drone system
content: Hanwha Aerospace and Lockheed Martin UK have unveiled a new version of the Redback infantry fighting vehicle (IFV) combining a British-built 40mm turret with counter-drone technology.The companies presented the configuration at Defense Vehicle Dynamics 2026 in Millbrook, England, as they look to offer the Redback to NATO countries seeking to modernize armored and reconnaissance forces.A different Redback for NATOThe new vehicle retains the tracked Redback hull but replaces the configuration selected by Australia with Lockheed Martin UK’s crewed turret. The turret carries a CTA International 40mm cannon, giving the vehicle a different weapons setup from the Australian Redback’s 30mm cannon.The turret was developed and integrated at Lockheed Martin UK’s Bedfordshire facility. The choice of the 40mm weapon also gives the vehicle access to a range of NATO-qualified ammunition. Hanwha’s Byunggil Lee said the company selected the cannon for the flexibility its ammunition types provide.The Australian Army’s Redback, by comparison, uses a Northrop Grumman Mk44S Bushmaster II 30mm cannon, along with Spike LR2 anti-tank guided missiles and other systems. Australia has contracted Hanwha Defense Australia for 129 Redbacks under the LAND 400 Phase 3 program.Turning the IFV into a counter-drone platformThe more significant change may be the addition of Lockheed Martin UK’s SkyKeeper command-and-control system. SkyKeeper is designed as a battlefield command-and-control system for ground-based air defense and counter-uncrewed aircraft systems (C-UAS). Lockheed Martin says it can combine information from multiple sensors and coordinate kinetic and non-kinetic effectors. It is also designed to operate through the UK’s Generic Vehicle Architecture.For the Redback, SkyKeeper has been integrated directly into the turret architecture for the first time. The companies say this gives the vehicle a dual role: conventional infantry fighting and counter-UAS operations.That reflects a growing challenge for armored formations. Small drones can provide persistent reconnaissance and can also carry explosives, forcing armored units to contend with aerial threats alongside conventional ground targets.Adding counter-drone command and control to an IFV could let the vehicle participate in a wider air picture rather than relying solely on its own sensors. However, the companies have not publicly disclosed the complete sensor, effector, or engagement architecture of the new Redback configuration.Designed for different customersThe new version is not intended to replace Australia’s Redback configuration. Instead, it gives Hanwha another configuration it can adapt to individual customer requirements.The company plans to conduct live demonstrations in 2027, including in Canada and South Korea, as they pursue potential NATO and allied customers. The approach also takes advantage of the Redback’s existing development. Australia selected the vehicle in 2023, and its 129-vehicle program is scheduled to be built locally in Australia.For Hanwha and Lockheed Martin UK, the new configuration is therefore less about creating an entirely new IFV than showing how an existing armored platform can be reconfigured around changing battlefield requirements.The combination of a 40mm cannon and integrated counter-drone command system gives NATO customers another Redback configuration to consider as armored forces increasingly have to defend against threats arriving from both the ground and the air.

title: Northrop's new air-defence gun tests 50mm rounds to stop drone swarms
content: Northrop Grumman has completed an aeroballistic test of a new 50mm projectile for Raid Hunter, moving its gun-based short-range air defense system further along the development path.The round was fired from an XM913 Chain Gun during a trial intended to validate its performance and collect flight data.The information gathered will support the development of a guided, proximity-fuzed projectile for Raid Hunter. The system is being designed to counter large, coordinated attacks involving cruise missiles, unmanned aerial systems, short-range ballistic missiles, and drone swarms.Trial delivers high-fidelity flight dataNearly every round fired during the test generated high-fidelity data, according to Northrop Grumman. The results also matched the company’s pre-test predictions and expectations for the projectile’s performance.The trial therefore provided a practical check of the projectile design while giving engineers information for the next phase of development. That work will focus on adding guidance and a proximity fuze to the 50mm round.A guided projectile would give Raid Hunter a precision component for engaging aerial targets, while the proximity fuze is intended to support interception without requiring a direct impact. Northrop Grumman is pairing this ammunition with its Bushmaster Chain Gun technology to create a high-rate defensive system.The combination is being developed for situations in which defenders may face several kinds of airborne threats at once. Rather than being limited to one target category, Raid Hunter is intended to respond to mixed attacks involving missiles and unmanned aircraft.Built to confront mass mixed raidsNorthrop Grumman is positioning Raid Hunter as a scalable and cost-effective way to close gaps in short-range air defense. Its mix of precision-guided 50mm ammunition and rapid gunfire is designed to defeat high-volume attacks that could put existing defenses under pressure.A networked system controller will connect Raid Hunter to sensors and the broader air defense architecture. This integration is intended to support the flow of targeting information and coordinate the system’s response with other defensive assets.Raid Hunter also has a platform-agnostic design, allowing it to be adapted to different host vehicles and operational needs. That flexibility could enable the system to protect military bases, airfields, and critical infrastructure without being tied to a single vehicle configuration.The broader objective is to reinforce layered defenses by providing another option for engaging threats at short range. Its architecture also leaves room for upgrades as aerial threats and mission requirements change.Part of a wider defense portfolioRaid Hunter was previously known as the 50mm Gun-Based Air Defense system. It now sits within Northrop Grumman’s wider Raid Defense Solutions portfolio, which brings together kinetic interceptors, AI-enabled command and control, sensor fusion, and high-rate firepower.The portfolio is designed to accelerate threat detection, decision-making, and coordinated engagements during complex aerial attacks. By linking sensors, control systems, and weapons, Northrop Grumman aims to give defenders a more integrated response to large numbers of incoming threats. Completion of the projectile test marks another step toward that goal.
